abstract.t: Many systems emit individually signed records — receipts, attestations, statements — and store them locally. Each record verifies on its own, but the collection proves nothing: records can be deleted, reordered, or created after the fact without detection. This document specifies the Checkpointed Local Log (CLL): a producer-operated append-only log that is a Merkle Mountain Range as defined by the COSE Receipts profile for Merkle Mountain Ranges, together with a small signed checkpoint that commits to the log's entire history. A checkpoint carries the content of that profile's Receipt of consistency — the accumulator and the consistency proof — inside a SCITT Signed Statement, so it can be registered with one or more independent Transparency Services without any change to them. A CLL upgrades a set of point receipts into a stream with provable order, contemporaneity, and completeness, and states precisely what it does not establish. It defines no new proof format, no change to SCITT Registration or Receipts, and no payload semantics.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: A signed record proves that its issuer produced those bytes. It does not prove when the record was produced relative to its neighbors, that no record between two others was deleted, or that the set presented to a verifier is the set that existed. In current practice, producers of agent receipts, decision records, build attestations, SBOM and other supply-chain artifact revisions, and similar records sign each record and store the results in ordinary storage — a "log" whose integrity rests entirely on the operator's word. A relying party examining such a collection cannot distinguish an honest archive from a curated one. The problem is payload-neutral: a stream of SBOM revisions and a stream of agent action receipts fail in exactly the same way, and this document treats them identically.

Transparency logs in the style of address this by publishing entries to a small number of large, centrally operated logs, where anyone can audit the whole. That model asks two things the local case cannot give: that the entries themselves be published to a log the producer does not control, which is unacceptable when the content is private; and that each record be registered with a central service as it is produced, which a producer emitting thousands of records a day will not sustain in cost or latency. The need is a construction that keeps entries local and private and still lets a relying party check order and completeness.

The Checkpointed Local Log occupies the middle position: the log is local and private; only a small checkpoint — a signed commitment to the log's entire history — ever leaves the producer. The local log makes the record set tamper-evident to anyone who trusts the producer; the checkpoint collapses that history, however many entries, into one commitment cheap enough to publish on every emission; and a Transparency Service whose published Registration Policy admits a checkpoint only when it is consistent with the one before is what removes "trust the producer" from existence and ordering claims.

(the "MMR profile") defines the Merkle Mountain Range (MMR) structure, its accumulator, and the COSE Receipts that prove inclusion and consistency over it. An MMR suits a local log: appends are streaming and never restructure earlier entries, and proofs are logarithmic. This document is a companion to the MMR profile. It takes the structure, the accumulator encoding, and the consistency proof unchanged, and adds what a producer-operated log needs on top: how entries become leaves, a checkpoint that carries the profile's accumulator and consistency proof as a SCITT Signed Statement , the discipline that makes a sequence of checkpoints meaningful, and the claims a relying party can and cannot draw from them. states the relationship in full, including the path from a checkpointed local log to full Registration at a Transparency Service.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
The terms tree size, accumulator, node value, consistency proof, Receipt of consistency, add_leaf_hash, leaf_count, peaks and consistent_roots are used as defined in .

Entry: a 32-byte value appended to the log, typically the SHA-256 digest of a signed record produced by the operator or received from another party. Entries are otherwise opaque to this specification. The binding between an entry and the record it commits to MAY be expressed using a declared digest context (e.g., ), including contexts that commit to already-signed bytes exactly as transmitted.
Log: an append-only sequence of entries held as an MMR per .
Log size: the tree size of the log's MMR: its number of nodes, not its number of entries. A log of 21 entries has log size 39.
Checkpoint: a Signed Statement committing to the log's state at a given log size, structured per .

Consistency Registration Policy: a Registration Policy (), published by a Transparency Service operated by a party other than the log operator, that admits a checkpoint only if it is consistent () with the last checkpoint that service registered for the same log identity.
Producer / operator: the party that appends entries and signs checkpoints. This specification assumes they are the same party ().
Log identity: the pair (iss, sub) carried in the checkpoint's CWT_Claims (). All continuity requirements in this document are per log identity.

section.name: Relation to SCITT Terms
section.t: This document uses the terms of . The party that signs a record is an Issuer, and a signed record is a Signed Statement (COSE_Sign1). A checkpoint is a Signed Statement whose Issuer is the producer and whose Artifact is the log. A service that registers Signed Statements and returns Receipts is a Transparency Service; a Receipt proves inclusion in that service's log, not agreement with the statement. The check a Transparency Service makes before registering is its published Registration Policy. Independence comes from registering the same Signed Statement with more than one Transparency Service. A party that independently recomputes checks over records it is given works in the manner of an Auditor. SCITT defines no "witness" role and this document defines none; earlier revisions of this document used that word for what is now a Transparency Service applying a Consistency Registration Policy. One party signing another operator's log head is a separate layer outside SCITT and outside this document.

section.name: The Log Discipline

li.t: Append at production time. An entry SHOULD be appended when the record it commits to is produced or received, not batched for later assembly. The evidentiary difference is the point of this document: an entry appended at time t is committed by every subsequent checkpoint, so contemporaneity becomes checkable; end-of-period assembly permits curation that no later verification can detect.
Append-only. Entries MUST NOT be modified or removed. Erasure of the content an entry commits to is a separate act on separate storage and does not touch the log; the entry (a digest) remains.

One log, one signing identity. A log's checkpoints are signed under one key at a time. Key rotation is announced by an entry declaring the rotation — produced under the outgoing key and naming the incoming key identifier — appended before the first checkpoint signed under the new key. The log identity () is unchanged by rotation.

section.t: Segmentation and archival (non-normative). A conforming implementation MAY store the log as a sequence of segments rather than one unbounded file. This specification imposes no segment format; the only checkpoint-relevant discipline is that any segment boundary a producer defines SHOULD coincide with a checkpoint boundary, never a calendar boundary: closing a segment at the log's state at a checkpoint's declared size means the segment plus that checkpoint is independently verifiable without the rest of the log, using inclusion proofs against the checkpoint's accumulator. A store's own manifest of which segments exist, and whether each is presently retrievable ("mounted") or has been archived elsewhere, is local bookkeeping, not itself evidence a verifier trusts — only a checkpoint (and what it commits to) carries that property. A verifier presented with a reference to an entry whose segment is not presently retrievable receives a distinct, honest refusal (e.g., "retention expired") rather than being told the entry never existed, since the checkpoint chain already proves it did.

section.name: The Log Structure
section.t: A CLL is an MMR as specified by , with verifiable data structure algorithm MMR_SHA256: SHA-256 node values, interior nodes formed by hash_pospair64, and nodes added by add_leaf_hash. This document changes none of that. It fixes only what the profile leaves to the application, the leaf value:

where entry is exactly 32 bytes. The leaf value is the input f to add_leaf_hash. The leaf pre-image is therefore 33 bytes beginning with 0x00, which no interior pre-image (72 bytes, beginning with a position) can equal. This is the leaf commitment the MMR profile's Security Considerations recommend for applications that need leaves distinguishable from interior nodes.

The log size is always a complete MMR size: add_leaf_hash returns one after every append, and a checkpoint is only ever taken between appends. The number of entries at log size s is leaf_count(s - 1) (0 when s is 0).

section.name: The Checkpoint
section.t: A checkpoint is a COSE_Sign1 with an attached payload. The payload is a CBOR map with text-string keys, encoded deterministically (), with the following claims:

tr.td: the log size: the MMR tree size (node count) the checkpoint commits to
OPTIONAL: the number of entries, leaf_count(log_size - 1)
the accumulator at log_size, encoded per
log_size of this log's previous checkpoint; 0 for the first
the previous checkpoint's commitment; zero-length for the first
the MMR profile consistency proof from prev_size to log_size (); present if and only if 0 < prev_size < log_size
OPTIONAL: declared maximum seconds between checkpoints ()

section.t: The protected header carries the signature algorithm, the key identifier of the log's signing identity, and the CWT_Claims of . Additional claims MAY be present; verifiers MUST ignore claims they do not understand.
log_size and prev_size are tree sizes in the sense of the MMR profile. They count nodes, not entries. A producer that wants to state the entry count carries it in leaf_count, never in log_size.

section.name: Commitment Encoding
section.t: commitment and prev_commitment carry the MMR profile accumulator for their size: the node values of the peaks, concatenated in descending height order (tallest first), with no length prefix, separator, or further combination. For MMR_SHA256 each node value is 32 bytes, so the encoding is 32 times the number of peaks long, and the empty log (size 0) has a zero-length commitment.

These are exactly the bytes specifies as the detached payload of a Receipt of consistency for that size. A verifier recovers the accumulator by splitting the value into 32-byte node values; the number of node values is fixed by the size and MUST match it.

An implementation MAY additionally fold the accumulator into a single "bagged root" for its own fast comparisons between local log states. No such fold is specified by this document or by the MMR profile, and a bagged root MUST NOT be carried in commitment or prev_commitment.

section.name: Consistency Proof
section.t: When 0 < prev_size < log_size, the checkpoint MUST carry consistency_proof, whose value is the MMR profile's consistency-proof:
section.artwork: consistency-proof = bstr .cbor consistency-proof-content consistency-proof-content = [ tree-size-1: uint, ; = prev_size tree-size-2: uint, ; = log_size consistency-paths: [ * consistency-path ], right-peaks: [ * hash ] ]
section.t: as defined in . It is the same proof a Receipt of consistency carries in its unprotected header, here carried inside the signed payload. When prev_size is 0, or when prev_size equals log_size (the log did not grow between checkpoints), consistency_proof MUST be absent.

Carrying the proof in the checkpoint makes every checkpoint independently checkable from its predecessor with no further exchange with the producer, and gives a Transparency Service everything its Consistency Registration Policy needs in the Signed Statement it registers.

section.name: Checking a Checkpoint
section.t: A verifier holding a checkpoint and the public key of the log's signing identity MUST reject the checkpoint unless all of the following hold:

li.t: The COSE_Sign1 signature verifies, and the protected header carries CWT_Claims with text-string iss and sub ().
kind is "cll-checkpoint", and log_size, prev_size, commitment, prev_commitment and issued_at are present with the types of .
log_size and prev_size are complete MMR sizes, and prev_size is not greater than log_size.
The length of commitment is 32 times the number of peaks of log_size, and the length of prev_commitment is 32 times the number of peaks of prev_size.
If leaf_count is present, it equals leaf_count(log_size - 1) (0 when log_size is 0).
If prev_size is 0, consistency_proof is absent.
If prev_size equals log_size, consistency_proof is absent and commitment equals prev_commitment.

Otherwise consistency_proof is present and is a consistency-proof; its tree-size-1 equals prev_size and its tree-size-2 equals log_size; and applying the verification steps of the MMR profile for a Receipt of consistency — consistent_roots from prev_size and the accumulator in prev_commitment, followed by the right-peaks — yields an accumulator whose encoding () equals commitment.

section.t: Step 8 is the step a Receipt of consistency verifier performs before checking its signature, with prev_commitment as the trusted accumulator. It establishes that the log at log_size extends the log at prev_size without modification. It does not establish that prev_commitment is the commitment of a checkpoint anyone else has seen; that is the role of Registration ().

section.name: Required Constraints — Elected Once, Then Binding
section.t: Publishing checkpoints is OPTIONAL. Once a producer elects to publish, the following are REQUIREMENTS, because a checkpoint regime with discretionary gaps supports none of the claims in :

li.t: Declared cadence. The producer MUST declare a maximum interval between checkpoints (and MAY declare a maximum entry lag). The declaration SHOULD be carried in the checkpoint's cadence claim; however conveyed, it MUST be available to every Transparency Service the checkpoints are registered with. A missing checkpoint at any of them is thereby a detectable event, not an ambiguity. A producer with no new entries meets the cadence with a checkpoint whose log_size equals its prev_size.

Continuity. Each checkpoint MUST pass with its prev_size and prev_commitment equal to the log_size and commitment of the producer's previous checkpoint for the same log identity. This internal relation is checkable offline by any verifier holding the two checkpoints; it establishes that the presented history was not rewritten between them. It does not, by itself, establish that no divergent history exists: a forking producer can satisfy the internal relation on each fork separately. Detecting that requires state across time, which a single offline verifier does not have, and is what a Consistency Registration Policy adds ().

Named, independent Transparency Services. A producer representing a log's checkpoints as independently registered MUST name the Transparency Services it relies on and the Registration Policy each publishes. A Transparency Service operated by the producer confers no independence; it is a replica.

No claims beyond the last registered checkpoint. Entries appended after the most recent registered checkpoint are, to a relying party, exactly as strong as a log with no registered checkpoint. Producers MUST NOT represent them otherwise.

section.name: Checkpoint Registration
section.t: The checkpoint's protected header MUST carry the CWT_Claims header parameter with the claims requires of a Signed Statement: iss (the CWT Issuer claim ) identifies the producer, and sub (the CWT Subject claim) identifies the log. sub MUST be the same value in every checkpoint of a log, and MUST NOT vary per checkpoint: a checkpoint is a new Signed Statement about the same Artifact, which asks an Issuer to register under the same iss and sub. The pair (iss, sub) is the log identity every continuity check keys on. A sub that changes with every checkpoint (for example, one that embeds the log size) gives each checkpoint a new log identity, so a Transparency Service never finds a predecessor to check it against, and continuity is silently never enforced.

The checkpoint is registered as a Signed Statement per , by any transport the Transparency Service accepts. A Transparency Service unaware of this document can register it as an ordinary Signed Statement.

A Transparency Service applying a Consistency Registration Policy performs the checks of and, in addition, keeps for each log identity the log_size and commitment of the last checkpoint it itself registered. For a checkpoint whose log identity it holds state for, it MUST verify that prev_size and prev_commitment equal that state, and on failure MUST refuse registration and MUST treat the failure as evidence of log mutation, never as an error to be retried. For a log identity it holds no state for, it MAY register the checkpoint as the start of that log's history at the service; continuity at that service is then established from that checkpoint forward and says nothing about the history before it. This is the MMR profile's "empty tree as trusted state" case, applied per log identity.

The Receipt the Transparency Service returns proves that the checkpoint is included in the Transparency Service's log, and the time of registration if and only if the Receipt carries a signed time claim. A Receipt is an inclusion proof; it is not the service's agreement with the checkpoint. Continuity follows from the published Registration Policy: where that policy is a Consistency Registration Policy, inclusion under it shows the check passed. A Transparency Service that registers a checkpoint without the check returns a Receipt that proves inclusion and nothing about continuity. A verifier SHOULD know which Registration Policy the Transparency Service applied, and relies on continuity only when it does.

Scope of the Consistency Registration Policy. defines a Registration Policy over the non-opaque header and metadata of the COSE Envelope, permits the service to validate the payload of a Signed Statement (), and leaves the scope of checks beyond the mandatory ones to the implementation (). A Consistency Registration Policy reads the log identity from the protected header's CWT_Claims and the claims of from the payload. This document does not copy those claims into the protected header. Because the consistency proof is carried in the checkpoint, the Signed Statement itself is the material requires the service to make available for Auditors to reproduce its check.

Registering the same checkpoint with more than one Transparency Service () strengthens the log against equivocation (presenting different histories to different parties): an equivocating producer must present a consistent history to every one of them ().

section.name: Relationship to the MMR Profile
section.t: This section is non-normative. It states how a CLL relates to , what a checkpoint gives a relying party and what it does not, and how a CLL's entries can later receive full Registration at a Transparency Service.

tr.td: the producer, in a Signed Statement
Registration under a Consistency Registration Policy

section.name: A Checkpoint and a Receipt of Consistency
section.t: A Receipt of consistency for an MMR_SHA256 log is a COSE_Sign1 whose detached payload is the accumulator at tree-size-2, whose protected header carries tree-size-2, and whose unprotected header carries one or more consistency proofs. A checkpoint carries the same three things — commitment is the payload bytes, log_size is tree-size-2, consistency_proof is the proof — with three differences:

li.t: Signer. A Receipt is signed by the operator of the verifiable data structure in its role as a Transparency Service, over that service's own log. A checkpoint is signed by the producer as an Issuer, over the producer's local log. It is a Signed Statement, not a Receipt in the sense of , and it becomes transparent only by being registered.

Placement. The Receipt detaches its payload and carries the proof in the unprotected header. The checkpoint attaches the accumulator and puts the proof, log_size and the previous state inside the signed payload, so a Transparency Service registering it receives everything its Registration Policy evaluates in one Signed Statement, and the proof is covered by the producer's signature.

Previous state. A Receipt of consistency leaves the trusted accumulator to the verifier. A checkpoint names its predecessor (prev_size, prev_commitment), which is what lets a Transparency Service detect a fork or a skipped checkpoint by comparing it with the state it holds.

section.t: Because the bytes coincide, a producer that also operates its log as a Receipt-issuing service can issue a Receipt of consistency over the same sizes, and a verifier that has checked one has checked the other's accumulator. Nothing in this document requires that.

section.name: What a Checkpoint Establishes
section.t: Given one checkpoint, any verifier can check entries against it: an entry is in the log at a position (an MMR profile inclusion proof against the accumulator in commitment), and a presented range of entries is complete. Given two checkpoints of one log, any verifier can check that the later log extends the earlier one without modification (, step 8). All of this holds to the extent the verifier trusts the producer, because the producer signed every checkpoint and chose what to present.

Registered under a Consistency Registration Policy at one or more Transparency Services the verifier regards as independent of the producer, the same checkpoints additionally establish, against a producer the verifier does not trust: that each committed entry existed no later than the registration of the first checkpoint covering it; that no registered checkpoint was followed by a rewritten, reordered, or truncated history; and, across services, that the producer did not show divergent histories to them ().

section.name: What a Checkpoint Does Not Establish
section.t: A checkpoint does not make any entry transparent. A Transparency Service that registers checkpoints never receives the entries; it cannot be queried for a record, and verifying a particular entry still requires the producer (or another holder) to present the entry and its inclusion proof. A checkpoint says nothing about the truth of an entry's content, about whether the producer has other logs, or about records the producer never appended (). And a checkpoint is not a Receipt: a relying party that needs a Transparency Service's own signed proof about a specific record needs that record registered.

section.name: The Path to Full Registration
section.t: A CLL is designed so that its records can later receive full Registration without losing what the local log already proved:

li.t: Checkpoints only (this document). The producer registers checkpoints; records stay local and private. Relying parties get order, completeness, and an upper bound on creation time for every entry, at the cost of one small Signed Statement per cadence interval.

Selected records registered. When a record needs independent, per-record transparency — it is disclosed to a counterparty, or contested — the producer registers that record itself, as a Signed Statement, with a Transparency Service (). The record gains its own Receipt and becomes a Transparent Statement. Its CLL inclusion proof against an earlier registered checkpoint is retained as evidence that the record existed, in that position, before the later Registration; the later Receipt does not by itself establish that.

The log operated as a Transparency Service. A producer that wants every record registered as it is produced can operate (or delegate) its log as a Transparency Service whose verifiable data structure is MMR_SHA256. Its Receipts of inclusion and of consistency then come directly from the MMR profile, and checkpoints become unnecessary for that log; the continuity a Consistency Registration Policy gave is then given by Receipts of consistency verified from trusted state. The log's existing nodes need no conversion, since they were built with the profile's algorithms from the start.

section.t: Each step keeps the leaf values, node values, and accumulators of the step before it, so a relying party's earlier verification remains valid.

section.name: Profile Revisions
section.t: This document cites at its current revision, -03. The editors' copy of the profile differs from -03 in ways this document depends on: it specifies the detached payload of a Receipt of consistency as the accumulator's node values concatenated in descending height order (the encoding uses), it adds a protected tree-size-2 header to the Receipt of consistency, and it states consistent_roots with the exact proof shape checks step 8 of relies on. This document follows the editors' copy and will track the next published revision of the profile. The checkpoint carries its tree size in the signed payload, so it does not depend on the protected tree-size-2 header.

section.name: Verification
section.t: Given a checkpoint that passes , a verifier can check, using only the proof formats of :

li.t: Inclusion: a given entry is committed at a given position under commitment: the leaf value of and an MMR profile inclusion proof reach one of the accumulator's node values.
Consistency: a later checkpoint's log extends an earlier checkpoint's log without modification: step 8 of , applied across one or more consecutive checkpoints.

Range completeness: the entries between positions i and j under a checkpoint are exactly the presented set — nothing between them was omitted: an inclusion proof for every position in the range against the same accumulator. Implementations MAY use a more compact multi-leaf proof; this document does not define one.

section.t: Given a checkpoint registered under a Consistency Registration Policy, each of these claims additionally holds against a party who does not trust the producer, to the extent the verifier trusts that the Transparency Services are independent of the producer and apply their published policy.

section.name: What a CLL Does and Does Not Establish
section.t: A CLL whose checkpoints are registered under a Consistency Registration Policy establishes: that each committed entry existed no later than the first registered checkpoint covering it (contemporaneity); that the committed sequence has not been reordered, had entries removed, or been rewritten (order and integrity); and that a presented range is complete (completeness).

These claims come from what the Transparency Service registers, which is only checkpoints, not entries. A Transparency Service registering checkpoints receives commitments; it does not receive, index, or retain the entries themselves. Its log therefore records the shape of the committed history — existence, order, completeness of the committed sequence — and nothing about any individual entry beyond its membership. Two consequences a reader familiar with per-record transparency logs must not overlook: it cannot be queried as an independent index or lookup for a particular record, because it never held one; and verifying any individual entry still requires the producer, or another holder, to present that entry and its inclusion proof — the registered checkpoint is the commitment they resolve against, not the entry. A deployment that needs per-record lookup registers those records directly with a Transparency Service (, step 2 of the path to full Registration); that is a different trade — publication and per-record registration cost in exchange for independent per-record lookup.

A CLL establishes nothing about the truth of any entry's content. A log of false records with every checkpoint registered is still a set of false records. Whether a record's content is accurate, whether its signer was authorized, and whether any claimed real-world effect occurred are separate claims requiring separate evidence (counterparty confirmation, external corroboration), outside this document's scope. Producers and tools MUST NOT present registration of checkpoints as evidence of content accuracy.

A CLL likewise does not establish that the log is the producer's only log, nor that all records the producer created were appended. It bounds omission within the committed history; it cannot prove a parallel uncommitted history does not exist. Deployments for which that distinction matters bind the log identity to an accountable party by mechanisms outside this document.

section.name: Implementation Status
section.t: This section records the status of known implementations at the time of writing. It is not a conformance statement.

Four implementations (Python, Go, TypeScript, and Rust) maintained in one repository build the log of and agree, node for node, with the test vectors published with this revision , which are generated from the editors' copy of the MMR profile without using any of them. Each implementation's consistency proof maps onto the MMR profile's consistency-proof without loss. As of this revision, all four still emit the checkpoint wire form of the previous revision: the commitment as a CBOR array of node values, a consistency proof in an implementation-specific form, and a sub that varies per checkpoint. The vectors include tests that detect when each implementation adopts the form specified here.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The security considerations of apply.

Equivocation. A producer maintaining two divergent logs under one log identity must present each Transparency Service a consistent view. With k independent Transparency Services and a verifier that checks Receipts from any subset of them, sustained equivocation requires controlling or partitioning every Transparency Service that verifier relies on. The cheapness of checking a checkpoint (a logarithmic proof from the previous commitment, holding no entry data) is what makes registration with a meaningful number of independent Transparency Services economically plausible. Verifiers SHOULD require Receipts from more than one Transparency Service where the threat model includes collusion between the producer and a service operator.

Log identity. Continuity is enforced per (iss, sub). A producer that changes sub between checkpoints, or registers a checkpoint under a new log identity, starts a new history at every Transparency Service. A verifier SHOULD treat a log identity that first appears at a service with prev_size greater than 0 as a log whose earlier history that service did not check.

Declared sizes. The MMR profile notes that a consistency proof does not by itself fix tree-size-2. A checkpoint signs log_size in its payload and step 8 of requires the proof's tree-size-2 to equal it, so a presenter cannot choose the size a verifier records.

Backdating. An entry can be created with any internal timestamp, but its position in the log bounds its creation time from above by the first registered checkpoint covering it. The backdating window is therefore the declared cadence plus registration latency. Producers wanting a smaller window declare a shorter cadence.

Key compromise. A stolen signing key permits forged future checkpoints but cannot rewrite history already registered: a forged checkpoint inconsistent with a registered predecessor fails the Consistency Registration Policy. Each Transparency Service's append-only log retains every registered checkpoint, which is part of the security function.
Signature algorithm. This document defines no signature algorithm. New deployments using Ed25519 should identify it with the fully specified algorithm identifier of .

Cryptographic agility. This revision defines checkpoints for logs using MMR_SHA256 only. The node value size, and therefore the commitment length rule of , follows from that identifier. A log using another verifiable data structure algorithm registered for the MMR profile in the future would need a claim naming it; this document does not define one.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: A checkpoint reveals the log's size and cadence and nothing else; entries are digests, and content never leaves the producer. Deployments for which entry count is sensitive MAY pad with reserved entries; this document does not define a padding scheme. The privacy considerations of on low-entropy leaf pre-images apply to entries: an entry that is the digest of a guessable record can be confirmed by anyone who obtains an inclusion proof for it.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document makes no IANA requests.

section.name: Artifact Type Declaration for Payload Binding
section.t: This section declares, for use with , the digest context of the cll-checkpoint artifact type. It is a declaration by the owning specification, not an IANA registration.

dd.t: the log state a checkpoint commits to.
the value of the commitment claim of a checkpoint ( of this document): the accumulator at log_size, which names the detached payload of a Receipt of consistency.
SHA-256; 64-character lowercase hexadecimal, as the as-transmitted registration fixes.

section.t: The test vectors give this digest for every log size of the example log (commitment_sha256).

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps

abstract.t: This document defines a date and time format for use in Internet protocols that is a profile of the ISO 8601 standard for representation of dates and times using the Gregorian calendar.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

CBOR Web Token (CWT) is a compact means of representing claims to be transferred between two parties. The claims in a CWT are encoded in the Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) is used for added application-layer security protection. A claim is a piece of information asserted about a subject and is represented as a name/value pair consisting of a claim name and a claim value. CWT is derived from JSON Web Token (JWT) but uses CBOR rather than JSON.

The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

front.title: CBOR Web Token (CWT) Claims in COSE Headers

abstract.t: This document describes how to include CBOR Web Token (CWT) claims in the header parameters of any CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) structure. This functionality helps to facilitate applications that wish to make use of CWT claims in encrypted COSE structures and/or COSE structures featuring detached signatures, while having some of those claims be available before decryption and/or without inspecting the detached payload. Another use case is using CWT claims with payloads that are not CWT Claims Sets, including payloads that are not CBOR at all.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts

abstract.t: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts prove properties of a Verifiable Data Structure (VDS) to a verifier. VDSs and associated Proof Types enable security properties, such as minimal disclosure, transparency, and non-equivocation. Transparency helps maintain trust over time and has been applied to certificates, end-to-end encrypted messaging systems, and supply chain security. This specification enables concise transparency-oriented systems by building on Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) and COSE. The extensibility of the approach is demonstrated by providing CBOR encodings for Merkle inclusion and consistency proofs.

This document defines a new verifiable data structure type for COSE Receipts [I-D.ietf-cose-merkle-tree-proofs] specifically for use with ledgers based on post-order traversal binary Merkle trees and which are designed for high throughput, ease of replication and compatibility with commodity cloud storage.
Post-order traversal binary Merkle trees, also known as history trees, are more commonly known as Merkle Mountain Ranges.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

This document describes version 2.0 of the Certificate Transparency (CT) protocol for publicly logging the existence of Transport Layer Security (TLS) server certificates as they are issued or observed, in a manner that allows anyone to audit certification authority (CA) activity and notice the issuance of suspect certificates as well as to audit the certificate logs themselves. The intent is that eventually clients would refuse to honor certificates that do not appear in a log, effectively forcing CAs to add all issued certificates to the logs.
This document obsoletes RFC 6962. It also specifies a new TLS extension that is used to send various CT log artifacts.
Logs are network services that implement the protocol operations for submissions and queries that are defined in this document.

front.title: Fully-Specified Algorithms for JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE)

abstract.t: This specification refers to cryptographic algorithm identifiers that fully specify the cryptographic operations to be performed, including any curve, key derivation function (KDF), and hash functions, as being "fully specified". It refers to cryptographic algorithm identifiers that require additional information beyond the algorithm identifier to determine the cryptographic operations to be performed as being "polymorphic". This specification creates fully-specified algorithm identifiers for registered JSON Object Signing and Encryption (JOSE) and CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) polymorphic algorithm identifiers, enabling applications to use only fully-specified algorithm identifiers. It deprecates those polymorphic algorithm identifiers.

This specification updates RFCs 7518, 8037, and 9053. It deprecates polymorphic algorithms defined by RFCs 8037 and 9053 and provides fully-specified replacements for them. It adds to the instructions to designated experts in RFCs 7518 and 9053.

front.title: Canonicalization Declaration for SCITT Signed Statements

abstract.t: Independently written systems that anchor records to a SCITT Transparency Service repeatedly need the same construction: a canonical form of structured content, a content-addressed identifier derived from that form, binding to a SCITT Signed Statement and Receipt, and references that cite external artifacts by digest. This document, referred to as CPB, specifies that construction as declarations rather than as a payload format. A payload profile declares its canonicalization algorithm and exclusion set and thereby obtains a reproducible derived identifier. A CPB Signed Statement carries either the complete statement content as specified by RFC 9943 or a digest of content held elsewhere using the COSE Hash Envelope of RFC 9995. CPB also defines an abstract typed digest reference information model and one optional protected-header encoding, cpb-refs; a payload profile may instead define its own reference serialization. An IANA registry assigns the canonicalization algorithm identifiers that these declarations name. CPB does not define payload content formats, establish or require a universal artifact-type registry, or require either typed-reference carrier.

front.title: COSE Receipts for MMRs, editors' copy

section.name: Changes since -01
section.t: Wire changes (each is a break from -01 for producers and verifiers):

li.t: commitment and prev_commitment are the accumulator's node values concatenated in descending height order, the encoding the MMR profile's editors' copy specifies for the payload of a Receipt of consistency. -01 said "canonical-CBOR-encoded exactly as the commitment object" of the profile, which no published revision of the profile defines. A verifier reading -01 checkpoints sees a CBOR array of byte strings.

log_size and prev_size are stated to be MMR tree sizes (node counts), matching the profile's tree size and what every known implementation already writes. -01 described log_size as the number of entries. Added the OPTIONAL leaf_count claim for the entry count.

Added the consistency_proof claim, carrying the MMR profile's consistency-proof, REQUIRED when the log grew since a previous checkpoint. -01 required the proof to be "made available" without saying how.
sub is the log and MUST be the same in every checkpoint of a log, per . A sub that varies per checkpoint defeats continuity.

section.t: Other changes:

li.t: New : a CLL is an MMR_SHA256 MMR; the leaf value is SHA-256(0x00 || entry) with a 32-byte entry.
New : the complete list of checks on one checkpoint, including a checkpoint where the log did not grow.
states what a Consistency Registration Policy checks, and what a service does with a log identity it has not seen.
New : the division of labor with the MMR profile, a checkpoint compared with a Receipt of consistency, what a checkpoint does and does not establish, and the path to full Registration.

Aligned terminology with . Removed the "Witness" definition. The role is now a Transparency Service that registers checkpoints under a Consistency Registration Policy; added . Stated that a Receipt proves inclusion (and the time of registration only if it carries a signed time claim), not agreement, and carries no continuity meaning of its own. Replaced the multiple-witness text with registering the same checkpoint with more than one Transparency Service ().

Removed the direct checkpoint countersignature form (RFC 9338), the "Stub Countersignatures — Future Work" section, and the IANA sentence forecasting a COSE header parameter for stub countersignatures.
Removed the SHOULD that each checkpoint holder retain every checkpoint: a Transparency Service's append-only log already retains every registered checkpoint.
Added the cll-checkpoint artifact type declaration for payload binding, moved here from the payload-binding provisional registry.
Added Implementation Status, Privacy Considerations, and security considerations on log identity, declared sizes, and the signature algorithm.
New test vectors .

Clarified the commitment representation: named the bagged-root fold as an explicit, non-wire, implementation-internal alternative to the peak-list commitment, and stated the peak-list encoding as the required wire form.
Downgraded the stub countersignature section (removed in -02) from a normatively-specified mechanism to a Future Work note, and removed the corresponding IANA registration request.
No checkpoint claim names were renamed.
